conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: The claim is false as stated.** Capsaicin has not been shown to treat breast cancer in humans. Current evidence is limited to laboratory (cell culture) and animal studies, not proven clinical treatment in people.

**What the evidence shows:**

Multiple in vitro studies demonstrate that capsaicin can inhibit growth and induce apoptosis/cell-cycle arrest in cultured human breast cancer cell lines (e.g., MDA-MB-231, MCF-7, BT-20), and can modulate pathways like EGFR/HER-2 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7646934/; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0960327110396530; https://www.nature.com/articles/onc2009335.pdf). These are preliminary mechanistic findings in dishes, not evidence of efficacy in humans.

A 2023 review explicitly states: "The clinical value of per os [oral] capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative," while noting animal-model evidence that capsaicin-sensitive nerves can influence tumor growth—again falling short of proven human treatment (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/).

Actual human clinical trials involving capsaicin and breast cancer patients (CAPTRANE, QUCIP) do not test it as a cancer treatment at all—they evaluate topical capsaicin patches for managing chemotherapy-induced or post-surgical neuropathic pain in breast cancer patients, a supportive-care use unrelated to tumor treatment (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2024.1452099/full).

Notably, some animal data even suggest capsaicin can promote tumor growth in certain skin cancer models, underscoring that its effects are context-dependent and not straightforwardly beneficial.

**Bottom line:** No human clinical trials support capsaicin as an anticancer treatment for breast cancer; existing human trials address pain management only. The claim conflates preclinical potential with proven clinical efficacy and should be considered unsupported/false as commonly stated.
